Fig02.title: Included urban metagenomes by sample type, continent and sequencing platform
Fig02.interp: Municipal wastewater (2,254), transit surfaces (1,911) and built environments (1,449) dominate the 8,053 samples; Illumina platforms predominate. The matrix mix differs by continent, so any pooled 'urban' summary is weighted towards matrices that dominate particular regions.
Fig02.limitation: Limitation: Descriptive counts; platform families only.

Fig04.title: Availability of processed annotations and sequencing depth by sample type
Fig04.interp: Most samples have raw reads and metadata only; processed AMR tables are concentrated in community wastewater (DS02) and municipal wastewater. Median depth ranges from 0.22 Gbp (hospital wastewater) to 10.7 Gbp (urban soil), a 50-fold difference that alone can change detection frequencies.
Fig04.limitation: Limitation: Depth is total sequenced bases from repository records, not post-QC depth.
Fig04.revision: Revision: Useful evidence of depth heterogeneity (median 0.22–10.7 Gbp by matrix). Revise: one text overlap flagged (AUD-15); panel A legend should state 'absent bar = zero'.

Fig06.title: Phylum-level alpha diversity of Indian open-drain wastewater by city and season (site-aware tests)
Fig06.interp: Median phylum Shannon diversity ranged 1.17–1.43 and rarefied richness 94–96 phyla between cities. With sites as units, richness differed between cities (perm. p = 0.002) but Shannon diversity only marginally (perm. p = 0.054); season had no detectable effect within sites (p = 0.27).
Fig06.limitation: Limitation: Phylum-level diversity is coarse; sample points are repeated measures of 19 sites.
Fig06.revision: Revision: Statistics are site-aware and correctly reported. Revise: two text overlaps flagged; numerical results are carried by Table 6.2, so figure is supplementary.

Fig08.title: Bacterial genus diversity across urban matrices and food-related environments (ResFinder resource)
Fig08.interp: Genus Shannon medians: air 4.88, transit 4.88, surface water 4.24, municipal wastewater 4.06, food-related 4.06, built environment 3.95. After adjusting for study and depth, no matrix contrast was supported (p 0.14–0.73; study ICC 0.56), so apparent matrix differences are largely study differences.

Fig10.title: Abundance of the 30 most abundant CARD gene families by city and season
Fig10.interp: Thirty CARD gene families dominate abundance in all city-season cells, with consistent ranking across seasons; efflux and multi-class families (some with housekeeping functions) are prominent.

Fig11.title: Detection of clinically important ARG determinants by city, CARD/RGI (high-confidence and any-hit tiers)
Fig11.interp: City-level detection mirrors Table 6.4: sul and tet(X) are near-universal; carbapenemase genes are rare at high confidence, with Kolkata showing the highest NDM (8.2%) and OXA-48-like (36.7%) frequencies; any-hit bounds are much higher.

Fig12.title: Monthly total normalized ARG abundance by city, March 2022-March 2024
Fig12.interp: Monthly median total RPKM fluctuated within each city over 25 months; Delhi was the highest city in most months. The lowest point (Chennai, August 2023, 88 RPKM) rests on five samples with an IQR of 59–602, so single-month excursions should not be interpreted as signals.
Fig12.limitation: Limitation: Observed series, not modelled; site composition varies by month; no trend test performed.
Fig12.revision: Revision: Only longitudinal series in the evidence base; observed (not forecast) values. Revise caption: it states that site identities are not available, which is superseded by the AUD-11 recovery of 19 site labels; state the number of sites sampled each month instead.

Fig15.title: Spearman correlations between CLR phylum abundances and resistance-class abundances (DS02)
Fig15.interp: Spearman correlations between CLR phylum abundances and class-group abundance show strong positive associations, for example Proteobacteria with multi-class (rho = 0.82) and peptide/polymyxin genes (rho = 0.71), and negative associations, for example Planctomycetota with beta-lactam genes (rho = -0.49); each of these pairs has BH q < 0.001 (correction over 150 tests).

Fig17.title: Between-study heterogeneity of normalized ARG abundance by matrix (forest plot)
Fig17.interp: Study means within a matrix span up to about 1.5 log10 units (e.g., surface water 3.9–5.3), comparable to the spread between matrices; I² was 0.97–0.98 in every matrix with at least four studies. This is the main reason matrix contrasts are treated as study-limited.

Fig19.title: Principal component analysis of CLR-transformed prokaryotic phylum composition (DS02)
Fig19.interp: CLR-PCA of 21 prevalent phyla: PC1 36.4%, PC2 20.2%. Samples fall into four discrete clusters (silhouette 0.79) defined by low-abundance phyla (Candidatus Omnitrophica, Chlamydiae, Candidatus Eremiobacteraeota), weakly related to city (V = 0.30), not to season (V = 0.09) or depth, but associated with total ARG abundance (epsilon-squared 0.10).
Fig19.limitation: Limitation: Clusters may reflect site or processing batch; CLR exaggerates differences in rare taxa.

Fig20.interp: CLR-PCA of 13 class groups: PC1 35.1%, PC2 25.8%, PC3 17.6%. PC1 is driven by fluoroquinolone/quinolone (54.7% contribution) and glycopeptide (29.8%) genes, which together make up less than 1% of total RPKM; ordination therefore emphasizes rare classes, and city overlap is extensive.

Fig27.title: Exploratory classification of municipal wastewater versus other urban matrices from resistome class composition (grouped CV)
Fig27.interp: With whole studies held out, the random forest achieved mean ROC-AUC 0.70 (SD 0.18; 2.5–97.5 percentile 0.23–0.85) and balanced accuracy 0.59; logistic regression performed below chance (0.46). Allowing study leakage inflated AUC to 0.93, showing that most apparent signal is study-specific.

Fig28.title: Exploratory prediction of total normalized ARG abundance from phylum composition (temporal hold-out)
Fig28.interp: Ridge regression on CLR phylum composition explained 52% of variance in later-month total RPKM (95% CI 0.28–0.67; MAE 0.110 log10 units), versus a baseline R² of -0.02; random forest R² 0.32. Held-out-city R² ranged -0.04 (Delhi) to 0.41 (Kolkata) for ridge, so the association does not transfer reliably between cities.

Fig45.title: Sensitivity of key results to sequencing-depth thresholds
Fig45.interp: DS02 site-aware city tests remain significant for total RPKM and family richness across depth thresholds from 10 Mbp to 1 Gbp, although thresholds up to 500 Mbp removed no DS02 sample and 1 Gbp removed only one, so this is a weak test for DS02; ResFinder matrix fold changes keep direction at every threshold; binomial thinning to 1–2 million read pairs reduces gene richness, confirming that rare-gene detection is depth-limited.
Fig45.limitation: Limitation: Thresholds remove few samples in DS02.
